function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

     2|
     3|*Book 2 of The Lunar Foundation*
     4|
     5|## Chapter 1 — The Observatory Rising
     6|
     7|*Mission AI: "Book 2 — Chapter 1: Deep space observatory array online. Long-wavelength cosmic observations initiated. Base status: nominal. Crew readiness: optimal. The next phase begins."*
     8|*Elena: "We learned to survive. Now we learn to see."*
     9|
    10|The silence of the Moon had never truly been silent. Elena Vargas had learned that over the past six months—learned to hear the whisper of static from the base's instruments, the subaudible hum of the life support system, the faint crackle of cosmic radiation passing through the hull. But tonight, as she stood on the observation deck of the newly completed Deep Space Observatory, the silence felt different. It felt like anticipation.
    11|
    12|The telescope array stretched across the floor of Shackleton Crater like a mechanical flower opening its petals to the cosmos—hundreds of antennae arranged in precise geometric patterns, each one tuned to frequencies that Earth's atmosphere had been blocking since the beginning of life. Ultra-long wavelength radio astronomy, impossible from the surface of any planet with an atmosphere, was finally within reach.
    13|
    14|"First light in thirty minutes," Rajiv Patel said, his voice carrying the same reverent tone Elena had heard in cathedrals. He stood at the control console, his fingers hovering over the activation sequence as if afraid to disturb something sacred. "The array has completed its self-calibration. All four hundred thirty-seven elements are reporting nominal."
    15|
    16|Elena nodded, not taking her eyes off the starfield visible through the transparent dome. The Earth hung in its familiar place, a swirl of blue and white that had guided them through the long lunar nights. But tonight, she wasn't looking at Earth. She was looking past it—into the deep field where galaxies swarmed like fireflies and the echoes of the Big Bang still resonated.
    17|
    18|"We've spent six months learning to survive on this world," Elena said quietly. "Learning to grow food, to recycle every molecule of water, to protect ourselves from radiation and the vacuum. We've done what no humans have ever done before."
    19|
    20|"But surviving isn't the same as living," Rajiv finished. He stepped up beside her, his shoulder brushing hers. "And living isn't the same as understanding."
    21|
    22|"Mei was right, you know," Elena continued. "When she said we came to study the Moon, but the Moon was studying us. We've been so focused on what we're leaving behind that we forgot to look at what's ahead."
    23|
    24|The comms crackled. Diego's voice came through, slightly distorted by the distance to the main habitat. "Observatory, this is Command. We're showing green across the board. The science team is ready whenever you are."
    25|
    26|Elena pressed the transmit button. "Copy, Command. Stand by for first light sequence."
    27|
    28|She looked at Rajiv, and he nodded. His finger pressed the final key.
    29|
    30|The observatory hummed to life. On the main display, data began to flow—spectral lines, interference patterns, the signatures of hydrogen clouds and distant pulsars and galaxies so far away their light had been traveling since before Earth formed. A universe of information, previously hidden by the static blanket of Earth's ionosphere, was suddenly visible.
    31|
    32|"First light achieved," Rajiv announced, his voice breaking slightly. "We're receiving. My God, Elena—we're receiving everything."
    33|
    34|Elena stared at the data stream, at the ghostly images resolving on the screen. Somewhere in that torrent of information were answers to questions that astronomers had been asking for generations. The formation of the first stars. The nature of dark matter. The structure of the universe on its largest scales.
    35|

     3|*A Novel of Survival on the Moon*
     4|
     5|---

     7|# Waters End — Book 3 of The Lunar Foundation
     8|
     9|## Chapter 1 — The Morning Report
    10|
    11|The numbers didn't lie. They never did.
    12|
    13|Commander Elena Vasquez stared at the holodisplay floating above her desk, the blue-white text casting sharp shadows across her face. Sector 7A, Luna Base One. 05:47 UTC. The rest of the base was still cycling through sleep shifts, but Elena had been here since 04:00, cross-referencing the weekly water report against her own projections. The coffee in her mug had gone cold an hour ago, and she hadn't noticed.
    14|
    15|She'd hoped she was wrong. She wasn't.
    16|
    17|The aquifer depletion rate had accelerated by 7% over projected models. Seven percent. Not a rounding error. Not a sensor calibration drift. A genuine, accelerating loss that meant the timeline they'd been operating on—eighteen months of remaining water—was now closer to fourteen. Maybe less if the trend continued.
    18|
    19|Elena rubbed her eyes with the heels of her palms until she saw stars. She was fifty-two years old, old enough to remember when fifty-two meant something different than it did here. On Earth, she'd been a project manager for NASA's deep-space initiatives. A desk job with occasional site visits to Houston or Huntsville. Here, she was the person who decided whether forty-eight people lived or died.
    20|
    21|The display refreshed with new data. A subroutine had finished crunching the consumption curves against the extraction rates. The crossover point—when demand would exceed supply—had moved three months closer.
    22|
    23|Elena pulled up the base's water inventory. Two hundred fourteen thousand, five hundred sixty liters of potable water remaining. It sounded like a lot. It wasn't. Spread across forty-eight people, with daily consumption factored in, it was a countdown clock with no pause button.
    24|
    25|The door behind her hissed open.
    26|
    27|"You're up early."
    28|
    29|She didn't turn. She knew the voice. "And you're up late, James."
    30|
    31|Dr. James Okonkwo walked around to stand beside her desk, a tablet in one hand and a cup of something steaming in the other. He was thirty-eight, a decade and a half younger than her, but the circles under his eyes made him look older. The water crisis had aged everyone in different ways. In James, it manifested as a permanent exhaustion that no amount of sleep seemed to cure.
    32|
    33|"Couldn't sleep," he said. "Ran the numbers again."
    34|
    35|"So did I."
    36|
    37|"And?"
    38|
    39|Elena gestured at the display. "See for yourself."
    40|
    41|James studied the data in silence. His jaw tightened incrementally—a micro-expression that most people would miss. Elena didn't miss it.     42|
    43|"This doesn't make sense," he said finally.
    44|
    45|"Which part?"
    46|
    47|"All of it. The extraction rate from the polar ice hasn't changed. The recycling loop efficiency is within operational parameters—I checked every sensor myself yesterday. The consumption should match the projections within two percent, not diverge by seven."
    48|
    49|"Unless we're using more than we're tracking."
    50|
    51|James shook his head. "The flow meters are calibrated. Every liter is accounted for in the main system. I designed that monitoring architecture personally. I spent four years on those specifications."
    52|
    53|"I know you did."
    54|
    55|"Then you know it's accurate."
    56|
    57|"I know it's accurate based on the data it receives." Elena turned to face him fully. "But sensors only report what they're designed to measure. If there's a consumption pathway we're not monitoring—"
    58|
    59|"There isn't."
    60|
    61|"James." Her voice softened. "I'm not questioning your work. I'm asking you to question it. That's different."
    62|
    63|He held her gaze for a long moment, then looked back at the display. His jaw worked silently, the muscles in his neck tensing. She could see him running the possibilities through his head, cataloging every subsystem, every valve, every junction where water might be going unmeasured.
    64|
    65|"Fourteen months," he said.
    66|
    67|"Best case. If the acceleration continues—"
    68|
    69|"It could be less."
    70|
    71|"Significantly less."
    72|
    73|James set his tablet down and took a long drink from his cup. Coffee, Elena realized. Real coffee. One of the few luxuries they still had, shipped in the last resupply package six months ago. She made a mental note: when the coffee ran out, the morale problem would get worse.
    74|
    75|"The primary recycling loop operates at 94.3% efficiency," he said, almost to himself. "That's the theoretical maximum for closed-loop water recovery in a lunar habitat. I designed it to hit 96.7%. We never got there because of the lunar dust contamination in the condenser plates."
    76|
    77|"How much water are we losing to that inefficiency?"
    78|
    79|"About 1.2 liters per person per day. Across forty-eight people... roughly fifty-seven liters daily. We recapture some of that through the atmospheric condensers, but not all."
    80|
    81|"Where does the rest go?"
    82|
    83|"Hydrolysis. The oxygen generation system splits water molecules for breathable air. A small percentage of the hydrogen doesn't recombine in the Sabatier reactor—it gets vented as excess pressure."
    84|
    85|"So we're literally venting water into space."
    86|
    87|"We're venting hydrogen into space. The oxygen stays. But yes, the net effect is water loss."
    88|

She'd need to talk to him soon, and she already dreaded that conversation.
    90|
    91|"Pull the last six months of raw sensor data," she said. "Not the summary reports. Every individual reading from every flow meter, every humidity sensor, every condenser output."
    92|
    93|"That's millions of data points."
    94|
    95|"Then get Jean-Luc to help you. He's better with large datasets than either of us."
    96|
    97|James picked up his tablet, already making notes. "What are you expecting to find?"
    98|
    99|"I don't know." Elena turned back from the window. "But the numbers are trying to tell us something. We need to listen before they start screaming."

Every instinct told her to push forward, to replace the bit and continue drilling. But her analytical mind—the part of her that had made her a world-class geologist—told her that pushing forward without understanding the failure was just asking for a repeat disaster."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1600, "content": "Chen looked at the borehole—dark, silent, waiting. But we test on a sample first.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1652, "content": "Chen looked at the fragments of the failed bit, scattered across the analysis table. Each piece was a reminder of the difficulty ahead—and the stakes."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1856, "content": "No messages from home. No updates from Chen's drill. No word from Jean-Luc about the Section 7 recovery."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1940, "content": "Kowalski turned his head to look at her. \"And how do I do that? The water crisis is real. The numbers don't lie. Even if we recover the ice from Section 7 and Chen's drill works and Torres finds water in the lava tubes, we're still living on borrowed time. Eventually, something will go wrong that we can't fix.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1968, "content": "It was 02:00 UTC, and Mei-Lin Chen was alone in the geological analysis lab."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1974, "content": "In the meantime, Chen had been thinking."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 1998, "content": "Chen stared at the pattern, her mind racing through the implications."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2024, "content": "Chen's heart rate accelerated as the implications cascaded through her mind. Commander Elena Vasquez sat at the small desk in the corner, reading through Chen's analysis for the third time."}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2102, "content": "Elena set down the tablet and looked at Chen. \"You're confident about the lens structure?\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2104, "content": "\"Ninety-five percent confident,\" Chen said. \"The drilling telemetry, combined with the seismic data and the density readings, creates a consistent picture. The ice is the dominant material — roughly 70% by volume.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2118, "content": "Chen ran the calculations in her head. \"At the reduced penetration rate — 0.15 meters per minute, which I recommend to minimize stress on the coated bit — approximately one hundred minutes of active drilling. But we'll need to stop frequently to allow the bit to cool and to verify structural integrity. I estimate three to four days of continuous operation, with regular pauses.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2136, "content": "\"And if we don't drill,\" Chen said, \"we have exactly what we have now. The Section 7 ice will buy us two months. After that, we're back to the same problem, with no solution in sight.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2146, "content": "\"Chen?\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2154, "content": "Chen felt a surge of relief so intense it almost made her dizzy. \"Yes, Commander.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2160, "content": "She left, and the lab fell silent. No more.\""}, {"path": "/home/bob/books/Moon_Base_Series/Book_3_Waters_End/manuscript.md", "line": 2226, "content": "The base's main corridor was quiet.
